edges.description: Supplying wild-type NDUFA6 to the patients' own cells restores assembly, which is the demonstration that the variants rather than something else in those genomes cause the stall.
edges.limitations: Cultured skin fibroblasts, not brain or muscle, and three of four patients - no tissue was available from subject 4. The activity arm of the rescue covers only two lines, because subject 2's cells failed to grow. Retroviral and lentiviral expression is non-physiological in level and timing. And the rescue says nothing about whether restoring the subunit would help a patient: it is a pathogenicity experiment, not a therapeutic one.

edges.description: Complexome profiling resolves an assembly defect into a subunit-level map. It showed the reduction of incorporated NDUFA6, the concomitant loss of NDUFAB1, NDUFA7 and NDUFA12, the reduction of N-module subunits, and NDUFAF2 still bound to the stalled intermediate.
edges.limitations: Cultured fibroblasts rather than the affected tissue, and three patients. The readout is protein abundance across a native gradient, not a direct measurement of assembly order, so the prerequisite relationship the authors propose between NDUFA6 and the later subunits is an interpretation of the abundance pattern rather than an observation of sequence.

edges.description: Removing the subunit from the yeast enzyme reproduces the two things that matter for the human disease: the acyl carrier protein leaves with it, and ubiquinone reduction stops. It is also the source of the expectation that NDUFAB1 would be lost from patient complex I, which the human complexome data then confirmed.
edges.limitations: A yeast, and a yeast whose complex I differs from the human enzyme in subunit composition. The alleles are a clean chromosomal deletion and designed alanine substitutions, not the missense, start-loss and frameshift alleles the patients carry. Most importantly, the yeast result is about catalysis - ubiquinone reductase activity is paralysed - whereas the human patients have an assembly defect, so the two systems agree on the subunit's importance without agreeing on the failure mode.

edges.description: An engineered change in the orthologous subunit alters complex I catalysis at a distance, which supports treating NDUFA6 as functionally coupled to the enzyme's ubiquinone chemistry rather than as a structural passenger.
edges.limitations: The direction is opposite to the disease. This is a dominant suppressor allele that improves complex I forward activity, recovered in a screen for rescue of other complex I mutants; the human patients carry recessive loss-of-function alleles. The organism is a nematode, and the paper itself notes that outside the LYRM domain the primary sequence of NUO-3 has diverged across eukaryotic evolution, so residue-level correspondence to human NDUFA6 is uncertain. Nothing here models the assembly defect that is the human lesion.

nodes.description: Two damaged copies of NDUFA6. Six distinct alleles are known across the four children, and they span most of the ways a small gene can be broken. Subject 1 is compound heterozygous for c.191G>C (p.Arg64Pro) and c.265G>T (p.Glu89*); subject 2 is homozygous for the two-base deletion c.331_332del (p.Glu111Serfs*35); subject 3 is homozygous for c.3G>A, which abolishes the initiation methionine; subject 4 is compound heterozygous for the frameshifts c.309del (p.Met104Cysfs*35) and c.355del (p.Leu119Tyrfs*20). None of the six is seen homozygous in gnomAD.

nodes.description: Forward genetic selections in C. elegans for suppressors of complex I mutants repeatedly recovered G60D substitutions in nuo-3, the NDUFA6 orthologue. ClinGen cites this work as part of the experimental evidence supporting the NDUFA6 gene-disease relationship.

nodes.description: NDUFA6 is an accessory subunit of the Q-module, the ubiquinone-reducing part of the peripheral arm. Complexome profiling of the three patients with available fibroblasts shows a marked reduction of NDUFA6 incorporated into complex I. Its LYR motif is what binds the mitochondrial acyl carrier protein encoded by NDUFAB1, a binding first demonstrated by deleting the orthologous gene in the yeast Yarrowia lipolytica, where loss of the subunit removed ACPM1 from the enzyme and paralysed ubiquinone reductase activity.

nodes.description: Losing NDUFA6 takes its neighbours with it. Complexome profiling shows NDUFAB1 lost in the most severely affected patient and markedly reduced in the other two, and NDUFA7 and NDUFA12 lost from the subcomplex in proportion to the degree of NDUFA6 loss. The NDUFAB1 result is the one that was predicted: the LYR motif of NDUFA6 is what binds it. nodes.description: Assembly proceeds and then stops. Blue native electrophoresis of patient mitochondria shows reduced fully assembled complex I with subcomplexes present that are absent from controls, and complexome profiling identifies the stall point: an approximately 830 kDa intermediate consisting of the P- and Q-modules but lacking the N-module, with the late assembly factor NDUFAF2 still bound to it. NDUFAF2 retention has previously been seen when the N-module subunits NDUFV1 and NDUFS4 are mutated, and it is the observation behind the idea that NDUFAF2 release is a checkpoint in holoenzyme assembly. All other OXPHOS complexes were unaffected, which is what makes the deficiency isolated.
nodes.id: Stalled 830 kDa Complex I Assembly Intermediate

nodes.description: The tissue lesion, and it is imaged rather than examined. All four children had neuroradiological abnormality, but the distribution differs. Subject 1 had diffusely abnormal supratentorial white matter with brainstem and cerebellar white-matter signal change at 36 hours of age. Subject 2 had extensive progressive lesions of supratentorial white matter including the corpus callosum, together with basal ganglia, brainstem and cervical cord involvement, later showing partial cystic degeneration and white-matter volume loss. Subject 3 had increased T2 signal in the basal ganglia with a diffuse atrophic process on follow-up. Subject 4 had white-matter change in the corticospinal tract, brainstem and thalamus.

nodes.description: The aerobic yeast Yarrowia lipolytica is the system in which the function of this subunit was worked out, years before it was linked to human disease. Deleting the orthologous gene removed the acyl carrier protein ACPM1 from complex I and abolished ubiquinone reductase activity; replacing the LYR motif and an associated conserved phenylalanine with alanines did the same. A later study of the same organism determined the structure of an inactive F89A mutant and found long-range changes across a cluster of conserved loops at the interface between the Q-module and the membrane arm.
nodes.id: Yarrowia lipolytica LYRM6/NB4M deletion and LYR-motif mutants
